title: EMT Medications
body:
## The EMT-Basic formulary

| Drug | Indication | Adult dose | Peds dose | Route | Contraindications | Key side effects | Reassess |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Oxygen** | Hypoxia, `SpO2` under `94%`, respiratory distress, shock, CO exposure | Titrate: cannula `1–6 L/min`, NRB `10–15 L/min`, BVM `15 L/min` | Same devices, blow-by if mask refused | Inhalation | None in an emergency (relative: COPD retainer — target `88–92%`) | Drying, absorption atelectasis, rarely hypoventilation in retainers | `SpO2` and work of breathing every `5 min` |
| **Oral glucose** | Suspected hypoglycemia with an intact airway | `15–25 g` (one tube = `15 g`), buccal between cheek and gum | `15 g`, same technique | PO/buccal | Unresponsive, no gag reflex, cannot swallow, suspected stroke with dysphagia | Aspiration, nausea | Mental status and glucose in `10–15 min`; repeat once per protocol |
| **Aspirin** | Suspected acute coronary syndrome / chest pain of cardiac origin | `324 mg` chewed (four `81 mg` chewables); `160–325 mg` acceptable | Not given (Reye syndrome risk under `18 y`) | PO, chewed | Allergy, active GI bleed or ulcer, bleeding disorder, already took a full dose, under `18 y` | GI upset, bleeding, wheeze in aspirin-sensitive asthma | Pain score and vitals; document the time |
| **Epinephrine auto-injector** | Anaphylaxis; severe allergic reaction with airway or hypotension | `0.3 mg` IM (`0.3 mL` of `1:1,000`) | `0.15 mg` IM if under `30 kg` | IM, mid-outer thigh, through clothing if needed | None in true anaphylaxis. Caution: coronary disease, hypertension, elderly | Tachycardia, tremor, anxiety, headache, chest pain | Airway, lung sounds, BP every `5 min`; repeat in `5–15 min` per protocol |
| **Naloxone** | Opioid overdose with depressed respirations | `2 mg` IN (`1 mg` per nostril) or a `4 mg` IN device; `0.4–2 mg` IM | `0.1 mg/kg` IN/IM, max `2 mg` | IN, IM (EMT scope varies) | Known hypersensitivity only | Acute withdrawal: vomiting, agitation, combativeness; possible pulmonary edema | Respirations every `2–3 min`; repeat `q2–3 min` as needed |
| **Albuterol** | Bronchospasm: asthma, COPD, reactive airway | `2.5 mg` in `3 mL` NS nebulized at `6–8 L/min`, or MDI `2` puffs (`90 mcg` each) | `2.5 mg` neb (some protocols `1.25 mg` under `1 y`) | Inhalation | Allergy, tachydysrhythmia (relative) | Tachycardia, tremor, palpitations, nervousness | Lung sounds and `SpO2` before, during and after; repeat per protocol |
| **Nitroglycerin** | Cardiac chest pain; CHF/pulmonary edema in some protocols | `0.4 mg` SL tab or spray, `q5 min`, up to `3` doses | Not given | SL | SBP under `100 mmHg`, HR under `50` or over `100`, right-ventricular/inferior MI, head injury, PDE-5 inhibitor (sildenafil/vardenafil within `24 h`, tadalafil within `48 h`), already took `3` doses | Headache, hypotension, dizziness, flushing | **Blood pressure before every dose** and `5 min` after |
| **Activated charcoal** | Selected recent oral poisonings, only on medical direction | `1 g/kg`, usually `25–50 g` | `1 g/kg`, usually `12.5–25 g` | PO | Altered mental status, no gag, caustics (acid/alkali), hydrocarbons, ethanol, iron, lithium | Vomiting, aspiration, black stool | Mental status, airway; ready suction |

## Assist versus administer

EMTs **assist** with the patient's own prescribed nitroglycerin and metered-dose inhaler, and **administer** oxygen, oral glucose, aspirin, epinephrine, naloxone and nebulized albuterol where the state authorizes it. The line between the two is a state and protocol question, not a national one.

## The six rights

1. Right **patient**
2. Right **medication** (check the label three times; check expiration and clarity)
3. Right **dose**
4. Right **route**
5. Right **time**
6. Right **documentation** (drug, dose, route, time, who gave it, response)

Many services add the right to **refuse** and the right **education** of the patient.

> **Key:** Every drug you give needs a set of vitals before and after. Nitroglycerin needs a blood pressure before *each* dose — that is the one people skip.

## New Jersey and state expansions

Scope is set by the state, then narrowed or widened by your agency's standing orders and medical director. In New Jersey, EMTs work under the NJ OEMS statewide protocol and, depending on agency authorization and training, may carry naloxone, epinephrine (auto-injector and in check-and-inject vial/syringe programs), nebulized albuterol, aspirin, oral glucose, oxygen, CPAP, tourniquets and hemostatic dressings.

> **On shift:** "Per protocol" is the honest answer on the exam and in the truck. Know your own standing orders cold; assume nothing from a textbook printed in another state.
